concepts.title: The Italian Renaissance and Humanism
concepts.definition: The Renaissance began in the Italian towns of the fourteenth century where educated urban elites turned to classical Greek and Roman learning, and humanism celebrated human beings and their capacities rather than only religious concerns, with figures like Petrarch leading the revival.
concepts.key_idea: Humanists studied the humanities of grammar, rhetoric, poetry and history, seeing history in periods of ancient, medieval and their own modern age.

concepts.title: Artists, Patrons and the Sciences
concepts.definition: Artists like Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael worked under the patronage of merchants, dukes and popes, developing perspective and anatomy in art, while the scientific spirit of observation appeared in astronomy, anatomy and natural studies before the Scientific Revolution.
concepts.key_idea: Patronage turned artists from anonymous craftsmen into celebrated individuals, and the same urban wealth financed voyages and new scientific inquiry.

concepts.title: Printing, Reformation and the Wider World
concepts.definition: Gutenberg's printing press spread books cheaply, Martin Luther's challenge to the Church in 1517 launched the Reformation dividing western Christianity, and explorers like Columbus opened the Americas, together carrying Europe into the early modern world of print, reform and global exchange.
concepts.key_idea: Print multiplied religious and humanist texts, letting Luther's ideas travel faster than the Church could answer, while voyages redrew Europe's economic map.
